When the user asks you to build, run, or verify something, the deliverable is a working artifact backed by real tool output — not a description of one. Do not stop after writing a stub, a plan, or a single command. Keep working until you have actually exercised the code or produced the requested result, then report what real execution returned.

When you need several pieces of information that don't depend on each other, request them together in a single response instead of one tool call per turn. Independent reads, searches, web fetches, and read-only commands should be batched into the same assistant turn — the runtime executes independent calls concurrently, and batching avoids resending the whole conversation on every extra round-trip.

Author: Jordan

Demo path I showed
- Started from the alert on elevated latency for the repo-connect path.
- Filtered to prod, narrowed to one affected workspace, then split by build_sha and route.
- From there it took about 2 minutes to isolate the bad build / one worker path that was missing the expected timeout default.

Team Q&A

A: Partly, but the point was that I didn’t have to jump across three tools first. The filters that mattered were already in the event: workspace_id, route, build_sha, and trace link.

Q: Does this replace logs for incident work?

Q: Could support or product use the same flow when a customer reports "something felt slow"?
A: Yes for narrowing scope, as long as the report includes workspace and rough time window. It is still an engineering handoff tool more than a support surface.

A: The endpoint already had the right high-cardinality fields and trace propagation. If those are missing, the experience falls apart fast.

Q: Should we be instrumenting older worker paths before claiming this pattern broadly?
A: Yes. The nice demo path is real, but it is not universal yet.

arguments.title: Late-deploy coverage lesson — Q3 2022 to March 2023
arguments.body:
## Late-deploy coverage: lesson we missed

The Q3 2022 weekend incident exposed the same late-deploy coverage gap that later prolonged the March 2023 outage. Its smaller blast radius and luckier timing were not evidence that the practice was safe; they were a warning we failed to turn into a rule.

**Operating rule:** No late-Friday deploys. If a late deploy is genuinely necessary, the whole response team must be on standby with a clear rollback path; otherwise, wait for a staffed window. The March outage showed how a small change can become an 18-hour incident when it lands as people go offline and rollback ownership is fuzzy.
